finding: `TP_RUN_DIR` is the anchor for every per-unit artifact path in the spec (`$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-baseline.json` §3.1, `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json` §5.2, `TP_ROUND_DIR = $TP_RUN_DIR/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND` §3.1), but its value is never defined. §3.5 only defines the *log* path `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`; it never says `TP_RUN_DIR` is `.tp/runs/<run-id>`, never says whether it is absolute or repo-relative, and never defines the format of `<run-id>`. The Stop hook (§6.2) and `tp escalate` resolve paths from it in a child whose working directory the spec never pins, so a relative value and a child cwd other than the repo root silently write artifacts the driver will not find.
suggestion: State in §3.1 that `TP_RUN_DIR` is the absolute path of `.tp/runs/<run-id>`, give `<run-id>`'s format (e.g. RFC3339-derived or ULID) and its filename-safety constraint, and state the working directory children are spawned in.

finding: `tp run [spec]` accepts the same optional spec argument and `--file` flag as `tp resume`, but nothing in the spawn contract passes that selection to the child. The fixed env list is `TP_RUN_ID`, `TP_UNIT_ID`, `TP_UNIT_KIND`, `TP_UNIT_SEQ`, `TP_ROUND`, `TP_RUN_DIR`, `TP_ROUND_DIR`, and `{prompt}` only names the unit's `brief_command`. A child running `tp next` / `tp review` / `tp done` therefore falls back to discovery or the `.tp/local.json` active pointer, which can resolve to a different task file than the one the driver was pointed at — the driver would then re-read cycle state for file A while its child closed a task in file B, and the durable-write predicates in §3.3 would never fire.
suggestion: Either require the driver to append the resolved task file to every unit's brief/prompt and export it (e.g. `TP_FILE`), or state explicitly that `tp run` refuses a spec/`--file` argument that is not the active pointer.

finding: Round 3 gave TP_RUNNER a fixed positional arg list ending in `{max_budget_usd}`, but the same subsection states that a resolved `run_max_unit_budget_usd` of 0 means the flag is omitted "rather than passing a literal 0", and that "a placeholder the driver cannot resolve is a usage error (exit 2) raised before any child is spawned". §7 gives `run_max_unit_budget_usd` the default 0, so at defaults the test seam's `{max_budget_usd}` either expands to the literal 0 the spec just forbade or is unresolvable and exits 2 before any fake child runs — which would make the seam unusable on the default path it exists to test.
suggestion: State explicitly what `{max_budget_usd}` expands to when the resolved value is 0 for a runner whose args are positional (e.g. it expands to `0` and only the claude template's flag pair is dropped), and say that a resolvable-but-zero placeholder is never a usage error.

finding: TP_RUNNER is declared to "outrank every other source of `runner`" and, in the same sentence, to be "the env layer of the existing precedence, so no new precedence rule is introduced". Those two claims cannot both hold: §7 puts `runner` in the layered path CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in, so under the existing precedence a CLI-level `runner` beats the env layer, and TP_RUNNER does not outrank it. Either the seam is a genuine new top layer (a new precedence rule, contradicting §7's "resolve through the existing precedence"), or a CLI source silently defeats the test seam and 10.2 test 16's "a CLI flag beats a task override" applies to `runner` too.
suggestion: Pick one and state it: either (a) TP_RUNNER is exactly the env layer and a CLI `runner` source outranks it — then delete "outranks every other source", or (b) TP_RUNNER is a test-only override above CLI — then say so explicitly in §7 as a documented exception, and drop the "no new precedence rule" claim.

finding: Two durable-write predicates cannot represent a legitimate no-change outcome, so a correct unit is indistinguishable from a crashed one. `audit-fix` requires `HEAD` to differ from `head_sha`, but CLAUDE.md's own audit rule blesses recording an out-of-surface finding with justification and no code change; `review-resolve` requires the spec hash to differ, but a round whose findings are all resolved as rejected/duplicate is recorded in `.tp-review/` (tp's existing --resolve writes the findings file in place) and leaves the spec byte-identical. In both cases §6.2's Stop hook blocks, the driver scores a failed attempt, the retry repeats the same correct decision, and the run ends with `unit-failure` — which §3.4 defines as "one unit exhausted its attempts". This also contradicts §1's "a driver that never accepts findings on its own authority": the driver effectively refuses the only non-accepting outcome.
suggestion: Make each of those two predicates a disjunction that includes the recorded no-change outcome — e.g. `audit-fix`: HEAD differs from `head_sha` OR the finding's row is recorded resolved-without-change; `review-resolve`: the spec hash differs OR the round's findings file shows every addressed finding resolved. Keep the baseline comparison for the delta half.

finding: Retries have no position in the six-step loop. §3.4 introduces `1 + run_max_unit_retries` attempts and §3.1 says the driver deletes the failed attempt's files before retrying, but the loop (steps 1-6) never branches on failure: it is unspecified whether a retry happens inside the same iteration (re-spawning the same unit immediately) or by falling through to step 1 and re-asking the oracle for `next_units`. That choice is behaviourally visible — a re-poll can return a different unit set, and caps are "evaluated between iterations only" (§3.4), so an in-iteration retry escapes cap evaluation entirely.
suggestion: Add the retry as an explicit step of §3.1's loop, stating whether the oracle is re-consulted and whether a retry counts as an iteration boundary for cap evaluation.

finding: Round 3 added `TP_ROUND`/`TP_ROUND_DIR` to the environment of *every* child, and defined `TP_ROUND_DIR` as `$TP_RUN_DIR/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND`. Four of the eight kinds in §3.3 (`implement`, `decompose`, `review-resolve`, `audit-fix`) do not run inside a numbered round, and the spec never says what `TP_ROUND` holds for them — so `TP_ROUND_DIR` degenerates to a path ending in `-r` with an empty component. §6.3 compounds it by keying behaviour on presence: "when `TP_ROUND_DIR` is set, `tp review` and `tp audit` emit that same path", which is now always set inside a run. The baseline file's `round` field (§3.1) has the same hole.
suggestion: Say that `TP_ROUND` and `TP_ROUND_DIR` are set only for the four round-scoped kinds and are absent otherwise (and `round` is null in the baseline for the rest), so §6.3's presence test stays meaningful.

finding: Round 3 restated identity as "an id is unique within its kind, so `(kind, id)` identifies a unit — which is the key `last_failure` clears on (§4.2)". That claim does not hold for three of the ids the same paragraph defines: `audit-fix`'s id is a finding index, which repeats every round; `review-resolve`'s and `decompose`'s id is the spec base name, which is constant for the whole cycle. So `(audit-fix, 3)` in round 2 and `(audit-fix, 3)` in round 5 are the same key, and §4.2's clear-on-match rule will clear — or worse, surface through `tp brief` — a `last_failure` recorded for an entirely different finding. The repair that fixed the record-kind collision left the rest of the table colliding.
suggestion: Either qualify the claim to the kinds where it holds and make the `last_failure` key `(unit_kind, unit_id, round)` for round-scoped kinds, or make `audit-fix`'s id round-qualified (e.g. `r<round>-<index>`) so `(kind, id)` really is unique.

finding: The per-attempt baseline file is written for every unit kind, but only three kinds read it. §3.3's predicates for `review-role`, `audit-role`, `review-record`, `audit-record` and `implement` are absolute (a file exists, a status is `done`); only `review-resolve` (spec_hash), `decompose` (task_count) and `audit-fix` (head_sha) are deltas — and all three are `Alone` kinds. So a parallel role fan-out of N roles makes the driver write N near-identical `$TP_UNIT_SEQ-baseline.json` files in one iteration that no predicate, hook or agent ever opens, and each costs a git rev-parse plus a spec hash at spawn time on the run's hottest path.
suggestion: Write the baseline only for the kinds whose §3.3 predicate is a delta, and say so in §3.1: 'the driver writes a baseline file for a unit whose durable-write predicate is a delta; absolute predicates need none.' §3.3's fourth column already marks which are which, so the rule is derivable from the existing table rather than a new knob. Test 18 then reads as 'a delta kind's predicate is measured against its baseline, and an absolute kind writes no baseline.'

finding: §3.1 says every child is spawned with `TP_ROUND` and `TP_ROUND_DIR`, but only the four round-scoped kinds (`review-role`, `review-record`, `audit-role`, `audit-record`) have a round. What `TP_ROUND` holds for `implement`, `decompose`, `review-resolve` and `audit-fix` is unstated, yet the paragraph immediately following says the driver "removes the failed attempt's files from the round directory" before every retry — a directory those kinds have no defined value for. §6.2's Stop hook uses `TP_UNIT_KIND` being set as its "inside a unit" test and reads `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-baseline.json` (run-scoped, fine), so the gap is confined to the round variables and to the retry-cleanup rule.
suggestion: State the value for non-round kinds explicitly — either `TP_ROUND` is `0` and `TP_ROUND_DIR` equals `TP_RUN_DIR`, or both are absent — and scope the retry-cleanup sentence to "the unit's artifact directory" so it is defined for all eight kinds.

finding: `{unit_id}` and `{unit_kind}` add a second delivery channel for two values every child already receives: §3.1 spawns every child with `TP_UNIT_ID` and `TP_UNIT_KIND` in its environment. Neither shipped template consumes them — the `claude` template's args are `-p/{prompt}/--output-format/...` and `opencode`'s are `run {prompt}` — so their only consumer in the whole spec is the `TP_RUNNER` fake runner. That is a test seam paying for two of the five documented placeholders, and every operator writing a custom `runner.args` now has to decide between two equivalent routes for the same fact.
suggestion: Either drop `{unit_id}` and `{unit_kind}` from the placeholder table and give the fake runner its identity through the env vars it already inherits, or keep them and state in §3.2.1 why a runner would need them on the command line when the environment already carries them — a real runner CLI that takes them as flags would justify the pair; the test seam alone does not.

finding: §3.2 was modified to give `runner` three shapes: a built-in template name, a runner object, or a per-kind map with a `default` key. §7's field table (unchanged) still describes `runner`'s range as "Built-in name or object", omitting the map shape entirely — so the field table a validator would be written from rejects the very shape §3.2 introduces the per-kind capability for.
suggestion: Extend §7's range cell for `runner` to "Built-in name, object, or per-kind map with `default`", and add an acceptance item in §10.2 for the map shape and for the missing-`default` usage error.

finding: `{max_budget_usd}` has no defined expansion when the resolved `run_max_unit_budget_usd` is 0. §3.2.1 solves it for the `claude` template only (the flag pair is not appended), but the `TP_RUNNER` seam's args are fixed as `["{unit_kind}", "{unit_id}", "{log_path}", "{max_budget_usd}"]` and any operator-authored `args` may place the placeholder as a bare token. §3.2.1 also declares that "a placeholder the driver cannot resolve is a usage error (exit 2) raised before any child is spawned" (asserted by test 10), so the default configuration of the very seam the tests depend on is ambiguous between expanding to `0`, expanding to empty, and aborting the run.
suggestion: State that `{max_budget_usd}` always expands to the resolved decimal value including `0`, and scope "unresolvable placeholder" to unknown placeholder names rather than empty values.

finding: §3.2.1 gives two rules that collide at the default configuration. The `claude` template omits `--max-budget-usd` entirely when `run_max_unit_budget_usd` is 0 "rather than passing a literal 0", implying 0 makes the value unrepresentable; but the `TP_RUNNER` seam's fixed args always contain `{max_budget_usd}`, and "a placeholder the driver cannot resolve is a usage error (exit 2) raised before any child is spawned". With §7's default of 0, the test seam therefore either receives a literal "0" (contradicting the claude rule's framing) or exits 2 before any child runs — which would make the seam unusable at default config and 10.1 test 1 unrunnable.
suggestion: Separate "unresolvable placeholder" (no such key exists for this runner shape) from "resolves to 0": state that `{max_budget_usd}` always resolves, expanding to the decimal value including 0, and that omitting the flag at 0 is a property of the `claude` template's arg construction only.

finding: §3.2 introduces a per-kind runner map (the producer/judge split) while §3.2.2 scopes spend reporting per runner: a runner with no `spend_key` "reports `spend: null` for its units, and `run_max_budget_usd` is inert for them". But `run_max_budget_usd` is a run-level accrued total (§3.4 `cap-budget`), not a per-unit setting, so a mixed map — `claude` default plus an `opencode` audit runner — leaves the cap armed while accruing only part of the run's actual spend. The cap then trips late or never, and the run-start "reported once, not silently" notice for a fully spend-blind runner does not cover the partial case.
suggestion: State the mixed case: either `cap-budget` is disabled for the whole run when any resolved runner declares no `spend_key` (and the start-up notice says which kinds are unmetered), or the cap stays armed and the notice must name the unmetered kinds so the operator knows the total is a lower bound.

finding: "`SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` set `interrupted` on the same terms: in-flight children finish" is not achievable with a default spawn. A Ctrl-C in a terminal delivers `SIGINT` to the entire foreground process group, so children receive it at the same instant as the driver and die mid-unit — leaving exactly the half-written durable state the design avoids. Making the stated behaviour true requires the driver to put each child in its own process group (`Setpgid`) or otherwise detach it, which the spec never says.
suggestion: State that children are spawned in their own process group so a terminal signal reaches only the driver, and say what happens if a second signal arrives while children are still finishing.

finding: `cap-units` fires when "executed units reached `run_max_units`", but §3.1 says `seq` counts unit *attempts* and §3.5's `units[]` rows carry an `attempt` field, so a retried unit produces two rows. Whether `totals.units` and the `run_max_units` comparison count attempts or distinct `(kind, id)` units is never stated, and with `run_max_unit_retries` up to 5 the two readings differ by up to 6x.
suggestion: State which the cap counts (attempts is the safer bound) and define `totals.units` in §3.5 in the same terms, so the run-state field and the cap cannot drift.

finding: `TP_RUN_DIR` is addressed by four sections (§3.1 baseline file, §5.2 escalation record, §6.2 Stop-hook predicates, §6.3 the reviewer/auditor write allowlist) but is never bound to a filesystem location. §3.5 defines only the log path literally (`.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`) and never says that directory is `TP_RUN_DIR`. This is load-bearing, not cosmetic: §6.2 denies writes to `.tp-review/` contents while §6.3 grants the role agent exactly one write under `$TP_ROUND_DIR`, and whether those two rules conflict depends entirely on where `TP_RUN_DIR` sits; 10.2 test 15's git-ignore list (`.tp/run.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/last_failure.json`) also only covers the run artifacts if `TP_RUN_DIR` is under `.tp/runs/`.
suggestion: Define it once in §3.5: `TP_RUN_DIR` is `.tp/runs/<run-id>/`, `TP_ROUND_DIR` is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND`, and both are covered by the shipped `.tp/.gitignore` — then state that no run artifact ever lands under `.tp-review/`, so §6.2's deny and §6.3's allowlist cannot overlap.

finding: `tp run --status` is required to print "phase, units done, spend against each cap, the last unit's exit code and log path" and, on an audit-phase stop, `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` / `role_streaks` / `divergence` "verbatim from `tp audit --status`". Neither `phase` nor the resolved cap values appear in `.tp/run.json`'s schema, and §3.5 forbids treating that file as truth. For a *stopped* run the phase and the divergence signals must therefore be re-derived from cycle state at status time — which needs the spec/task-file selection the stopped run used, itself not recorded (see §3.1). An implementer cannot tell whether to persist the phase or to re-derive it.
suggestion: Add `phase`, the resolved cap values and the task-file base to `.tp/run.json`'s schema as reporting-only fields, or state explicitly that `--status` re-derives them by re-invoking the oracle and name the file it uses.

finding: §4.1 states that `next_action`'s `command`, `brief_command` and `payload` "render `next_units[0]` when the array is non-empty", i.e. next_action becomes a projection of the unit array. §8a then requires next_action's mechanize branch (precedence step 3) to name a mechanize-candidate class and carry a phase qualifier — content that is advice about the review loop, not a rendering of any unit in `next_units`. Both cannot hold for the same non-empty array: either the mechanize branch survives and next_action is not a pure projection, or the projection wins and the §8a qualifier is unreachable exactly when review units are pending, which is the only time it matters.
suggestion: Say which fields the projection covers and which stay branch-owned — e.g. `command`/`brief_command`/`payload` render `next_units[0]` while `summary`/the mechanize advisory remain next_action's own precedence output — and cross-reference that split from §8a.

finding: `last_failure` has no owning writer. "tp records a `last_failure` object" covers two different processes: a non-zero child exit is only observable to the driver, while "closes with a failed quality gate" happens inside the child's own `tp done`. The clear rule ("a success clears it only when `(unit_kind, unit_id)` matches") likewise names no actor — the driver knows the pair from the unit it spawned, a child knows it only from env. Unlike `.tp/run.json` (§3.5, explicitly temp+rename because siblings write concurrently) and unlike the escalation record (§5.2, deliberately per-unit so siblings never clobber), `.tp/last_failure.json` is a single object with no stated atomicity or lock while concurrent role units can fail simultaneously.
suggestion: Name the writer and the clearer for each of the two trigger conditions, and require the same atomic temp+rename §3.5 requires for `.tp/run.json`.

finding: The unattended fence lists exactly three operations, but only two of them can manufacture convergence, and the field that most directly can is absent: `tp set --workflow` over the convergence policy itself — `review_converge_on` (severity threshold) and the clean-round counts — is not fenced. Lowering `review_converge_on` to `critical` or setting the required clean rounds to 1 produces the forged-approval outcome §5.1 names ("an agent that raises its own round budget and then declares convergence") without touching `review_max_rounds`. The `.tp/config.json` write denial in §6.2 does not close this, since these are set through tp's own CLI, which §6.2 deliberately leaves outside the matcher.
suggestion: Extend the §5.1 table to any `tp set --workflow` write that loosens the resolved convergence policy, with the same equal-or-stricter exception the cap rows already carry.

finding: The Stop hook's predicate now reads "the durable write is the condition that kind names in §3.3's fourth column". §3.3's table is `| Kind | Ends in | Durable write | Concurrency |` — the durable write is the third column; the fourth is Concurrency. Both sections were edited in round 3, and the column reference did not follow §3.3's shape.
suggestion: Refer to §3.3's `Durable write` column by name rather than by ordinal, so a future column insertion cannot desynchronise the two sections again.

finding: `location_clusters` is declared 'reporting only' — convergence arithmetic, the stored `clean` flag and `--status --check` are all unchanged — yet nothing scopes what it costs. Two problems for the agent that parses `tp review --merge`: (a) `severities[]` and `count` are re-derivable from the merged records the same output already carries (the records hold `location`, `role` and `severity`), so the entry duplicates data byte-for-byte rather than summarizing anything the reader lacks; (b) §7's `--compact` rule covers only run state ('`stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped') and says nothing about the review surface, so a compact merge — the mode an agent uses precisely to save context — appears to keep a payload that by the section's own words feeds no decision.
suggestion: State that `location_clusters` is stripped under `--compact` (and, if it is meant for humans reading a stop report rather than for the merge consumer, that it appears in `--status` only). Reduce each entry to `{location, roles[]}` and let the reader derive severities and count from the records already emitted, or say explicitly which consumer needs the two derived keys and cannot compute them.

finding: Modified step 4 reads "spawn a runner process per unit — units marked concurrent together", which implies a per-unit concurrency marking. §4.1 (unchanged) states the opposite explicitly: "Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table", and `next_units` entries carry only `{kind, id, brief_command}`. The loop's own wording now suggests a field the oracle contract deliberately does not emit.
suggestion: Reword step 4 as "units whose kind §3.3 marks parallel are spawned together, every other kind alone", so the loop derives concurrency from the kind rather than from a mark on the unit.

finding: Round 3 introduced `TP_RUN_DIR` as the anchor for three new paths — the baseline file (§3.1), the escalation record (§5.2/§6.2) and `TP_ROUND_DIR` itself — but no section ever defines what `TP_RUN_DIR` points at. §3.5 defines the log directory as `.tp/runs/<run-id>/`; the equality is inferable but never stated, and §5.2 already keys `tp escalate`'s usage error on `TP_RUN_DIR` being unset.
suggestion: Define `TP_RUN_DIR` as `.tp/runs/<run-id>` where §3.5 introduces that directory, so the baseline, escalation and round paths all resolve from one stated definition.

finding: The baseline object carries four keys — `{head_sha, spec_hash, task_count, round}` — but no §3.3 predicate reads `round`. The three delta predicates read `head_sha`, `spec_hash` and `task_count`; the two round-file predicates are phrased against `$TP_ROUND`, the environment variable, and the round is already encoded twice more in `TP_ROUND_DIR`'s `-r$TP_ROUND` suffix and in the round directory's own name. A stored key with three copies and no reader is exactly the two-sources-of-truth drift §3.5 refuses for `.tp/run.json`.
suggestion: Drop `round` from the baseline object, leaving `{head_sha, spec_hash, task_count}` — the round travels in the environment and in the path, both of which the hook and the driver already have.

finding: `TP_ROUND` is added to the seven-variable child environment, but the stated justification — 'they are what let a unit address its own artifacts without the driver passing them through prose' — does not hold for it. A role unit addresses its findings file as `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`; a record unit merges `$TP_ROUND_DIR/*.ndjson`. Neither needs the round number, and §6.3 confirms the round-scoped path is what removes the two-filename problem. Its only readers are the driver and the Stop hook, both of which can read the round from cycle state or from `TP_ROUND_DIR`'s `-r<N>` suffix they already construct.
suggestion: Either name the consumer that needs `TP_ROUND` and cannot get it from `TP_ROUND_DIR` (if the Stop hook is that consumer, say so — a hook parsing a directory suffix is worse than an explicit variable), or drop it and define `TP_ROUND_DIR` as the single round-addressing surface, keeping the child environment at six variables.

finding: §3.1 step 4 says "units marked concurrent together", implying a per-unit concurrency marking, while §4.1 states the opposite: "Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table". No unit carries a concurrency mark, so step 4 describes a field that does not exist in `next_units` (`{kind, id, brief_command}`).
suggestion: Reword step 4 as "spawn one runner process per unit — kinds §3.3 marks parallel run together, every other kind alone", so the concurrency source stays single.

finding: §3.2.2 requires the run-level budget cap's inertness to be "reported once at run start, not silently" when a runner declares no `spend_key`. §3.4's per-unit cap gets no equivalent rule, yet §3.2.1 makes it equally inert for the `opencode` template ("no budget flag"): an operator who sets `run_max_unit_budget_usd` on an opencode runner gets no enforcement and no notice, which is the silent-inertness §3.2.2 explicitly refuses for the sibling field.
suggestion: Extend the run-start notice to both budget fields: report at run start every configured cap that the resolved runner(s) cannot enforce, naming the field and the kinds affected.

finding: The plugin preflight ("if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `0.35.0`, it fails with the install command") names no host: §6.2's hook table has three events and none of them is a preflight, `plugin.json` is described only as identity, and no exit-code or user-visible channel is given for the failure. Version comparison against `tp --version` is also unpinned for a dev build or a prerelease tag. Test 24 asserts only `claude plugin validate` and hook-payload fixtures, so nothing pins the preflight either.
suggestion: Name the event the preflight runs on (e.g. the `SessionStart` hook, before the orientation payload), the failure channel, and the comparison rule for non-release version strings.

finding: §6.1's preflight (plugin fails with the install command when `tp` is absent from PATH or older than `plugin.json`'s version, compared against `tp --version`) and §6.4's 10-second hook timeout are both stated as requirements but have no test in §10.4; test 24 covers only `claude plugin validate` and hook payload fixtures.
suggestion: Add tests for the three preflight outcomes (absent, older, satisfied) and an assertion that every shipped hook declares `timeout: 10`.

finding: "Every command's `Args` validator exits 2, matching §9's definition of a usage error" points at a section that contains no such definition — §9 is the seven Non-Goals. The only place the spec defines exit 2 as a usage error is §3.2.1 (and §5.2 for `tp escalate` outside a run). An implementer following the reference to establish which failures are usage errors lands on nothing.
suggestion: Retarget the reference to §3.2.1, or add an explicit one-line definition of "usage error = exit 2" and cite that.
